name: National Catholicism
summary: National Catholicism fused Spanish national identity with the Catholic Church as the basis of the state. It made Catholic doctrine the inspiration of law, gave the Church control over education, marriage and morals, and rejected liberal democracy, class struggle and secularism in favour of an authoritarian, hierarchical, corporatist order under a providential leader.

defeat-communism.rationale: Vincent (s7) describes National-Catholicism meeting the threat of the left with violence to defend 'the rights of God', treating communism, socialism and republicanism alike as the anti-Spain to be excised.

democracy-best.rationale: Saz (s9) shows National-Catholics seeing the challenge of democracy and socialism under the Second Republic as the last step in the fatherland's dissolution.

more-religion-public.rationale: Principle II of the Principles of the National Movement makes Catholic doctrine the inspiration of all legislation, and Fuero de los Españoles art. 6 gives the Catholic religion official protection; Vincent (s7) describes National-Catholicism as making religion and politics one.

national-church-status.rationale: Its core thesis fuses Catholic unity and the confessional state with an organic conception of the nation, giving the Catholic Church a special status.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: It rejects religious pluralism explicitly and holds that Spain is defined by one religious unity, so no rival interpretation gets legal equality.

religious-nation.rationale: Principle II calls the Catholic faith inseparable from the national conscience, and Vincent (s7) reports the episcopal claim that Catholicism is the innate religious identity of Spaniards.

restore-past-order.rationale: Zaratiegui and García Velasco (s5), following Botti, describe the counter-revolution as thoroughly traditionalist and bent on restoring the pious society of the past.

separate-church-state.rationale: It joins Catholic unity and the confessional state, and treats the nation as defined by its Catholicism, so it rejects separating state from religion.

scope: The Spanish National Catholicism (nacionalcatolicismo) of Francoism, 1936-1975, with its roots in the Catholic anti-liberal nationalism of Menéndez y Pelayo, Balmes, Donoso Cortés, Carlism and Acción Española (s5, s8, s9). The defining sources present it as the ideology identifying the Spanish nation with Catholicism, hegemonic in Franco's regime and distinct from, though fused with, Falangist national syndicalism (s2, s5, s6, s9). Excluded: the American 'National Catholic' bodies (National Catholic Welfare/War Council, Almanac, Educational Association), the Polish National Catholic Church, and French Fédération Nationale Catholique, which the downloaded books cover; they are other things sharing the words. Botti's wider European 'national Catholicism' (s8) is noted, but the Spanish form is the scope.
